<explanation>
Based on an analysis of the file tree and README, you’re dealing with a forensic analysis toolkit called Mobile Verification Toolkit (MVT). Its primary purpose is to enable the consensual forensic investigation of Android and iOS devices by gathering and analyzing forensic traces. Given that it has separate CLI commands (mvt-android and mvt-ios) and a well‐structured codebase with various forensic modules and artifact parsers, your system design diagram should clearly map out both the Android and iOS forensic flow as well as the common/shared utilities.

Below are the guidelines to draw the most accurate and detailed system architecture diagram for MVT:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • CLI Frontend: 
     - Two main entry-point commands: “mvt-android” and “mvt-ios” (located in src/mvt/android/cli.py and src/mvt/ios/cli.py).
     - Depict how user input is provided via these command-line tools.
   • Android Forensic Modules:
     - Separate modules for artifact extraction, backup analysis, bugreport parsing, and adb-based operations.
     - Highlight the “artifacts” and “modules” directories under src/mvt/android which include functionalities (e.g. dumpsys analysis, getprop, settings extraction, etc.).
     - Organize the Android modules into sub-components: ADB-focused modules, Android QF modules, Backup modules, and Bugreport modules.
   • iOS Forensic Modules:
     - Similar structure evident in src/mvt/ios covering backup analysis and filesystem investigations.
     - Include modules for backup handling, filesystem analysis, and mixed data (like calls, contacts, SMS, etc.).
   • Common Core Library:
     - The src/mvt/common directory provides shared utilities, configuration management, command helpers, and IOC checking.
     - This is the glue that allows both the Android and iOS pipelines to work in a similar fashion.
   • Data & Artifact Parsers:
     - Under src/mvt/android/parsers and additional files in ios (like the JSON data files in src/mvt/ios/data), represent how raw forensic data is parsed and transformed into analyzable formats.
   • Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) Integration:
     - Although not a separate module in the code tree, the README emphasizes the use of public IOCs.
     - Indicate external IOC sources and how they integrate into the forensic analysis.
   • Testing and CI/CD Infrastructure:
     - Include a box that represents the continuous integration system (the .github/workflows directory with multiple actions such as tests and release publishing).
     - Also consider a note about testing directories (tests directory) that verify the behavior of each module.
   • Deployment & Documentation:
     - Dockerfiles (for containerized deployments) indicate that containerization is supported.
     - Documentation (docs and mkdocs.yml) along with the readthedocs settings should be noted as peripheral but critical components.
     
2. Relationships and Interactions:
   • Draw directional arrows showing the flow from CLI commands to forensic modules. 
     - For example, the Android CLI command triggers a series of module calls (artifact extraction, module-specific checks via ADB, backup analysis, bug report processing, etc.).
   • Indicate the interaction between modules and their shared common library for configuration, logging, and command management.
   • Show how parsed artifacts flow from raw data inputs (for example, from device backups or bug reports) through artifact parsers and then to modules that interpret the forensic details.
   • For the IOC part, show an external dependency (or integration) that feeds into the analysis process.
     
3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • The design clearly suggests a modular architecture targeted at specialized forensic tasks.
   • Separate concerns: the Android and iOS analysis are distinct yet built upon a shared common foundation.
   • Emphasis on reusability (modules and common utilities are reused across different commands) and extensibility (each module/sub-module can be evolved independently).
     
4. Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Python is the primary language (as seen from pyproject.toml and the file structure).
   • Containerization via Docker (Dockerfile, Dockerfile.android, Dockerfile.ios) for consistent deployment.
   • CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions workflows) indicate automated testing and release procedures.
   • Documentation is built with mkdocs and hosted on Read the Docs.
     
5. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines:
   • For this forensic toolkit, emphasize the separation of concerns between the Android and iOS forensic analysis pipelines. 
   • Clearly overlay the CLI layer that serves as the user interface for launching each analysis process.
   • Depict how each forensic stage (e.g., data input, artifact extraction, module analysis, IOC matching) is achieved in a step-by-step sequence.
   • Differentiate between processing nodes (modules and parsers) and infrastructure nodes (such as CI/CD pipelines or container deployment configurations).
     
6. Visual Elements to Include:
   • Labeled Boxes: Draw a box for each main component such as “MVT CLI (Android)”, “MVT Forensic Modules (Android)”, “MVT CLI (iOS)”, “MVT Forensic Modules (iOS)”, and “Common Utilities”.
   • Directional Arrows: Use arrows to trace the flow of data from the user commands to low-level forensic processing modules, and finally to the output (e.g., forensic reports or results).
   • Color Coding/Shapes: Apply different colors or shapes to separate command interfaces (CLI), processing logic (modules/parsers), shared libraries (common utilities), infrastructure (CI/CD, Docker), and documentation.
     
7. Detail Level:
   • Map out as many individual components as possible from the file structure. For instance, split the Android module box to include “adb modules”, “androidqf modules”, “backup”, and “bugreport” while the iOS module box includes “backup”, “filesystem” and “mixed” modules.
   • Optionally add notes on how tests and CI workflows contribute to overall quality, emphasizing the importance of a robust testing framework.
     
By following these steps and incorporating the components and relationships described, you will produce a comprehensive and detailed system design diagram that accurately represents the architecture of MVT. This diagram will then serve as a helpful reference for understanding the various forensic tasks, module interactions, and infrastructure elements that make up the toolkit.
</explanation>
